speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: UNDERSTANDINGS REACHED IN DISCUSSIONS BETWEEN BRITISH AND CANADIAN REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I stated to the house that within a few days a report would be made both in this house and in the House of Commons in Great Britain with regard to the agreements reached for the supplying of food from Canada to Great Britain. That statement is being made in the British house to-day, and I am therefore making it here.
Supplies of food from Canada to the United Kingdom. Joint announcement of understandings reached in discussions between representatives of the United Kingdom and of Canada at the Ministry of Food, London, January, 1946.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce and I, with officials of our departments, visited the United Kingdom in January and had discussions with Sir Ben Smith, the United Kingdom Minister of Food, and officials of the ministry of food regarding British requirements and Canadian supplies of the major foodstuffs. The discussions took account of the recent announcement of the United Kingdom government policy in regard to home agricultural production and ,of the long-term prospects regarding supplies of the different foodstuffs.
2.	This exchange of views has resulted in understandings being reached between ^he British Ministry of Food and the meat and dairy boards of the dominion Department of Agriculture on matters which are set out below and are now being put into the form of agreements to be signed on behalf of both governments.
3.	Bacon and ham. The United Kingdom is prepared to purchase the maximum supplies which Canada can provide in 1946, 1947 and 1948. Canada has agreed to do its utmost to maintain these supplies at the highest possible level.
4.	It was agreed that the present contract for the calendar year 1946 should be extended to cover the import of a minimum of 350 million pounds into the United Kingdom in
1947	and 400 million pounds in 1948. The contract price for the balance of 1946 and for 1947 will be raised to $25 per 100 pounds f.o.b. seaboard for grade A Wiltshires. For
1948	the price will be not less than the current contract price of $22.50, same basis, and will be subject to later review.
5.	It was agreed to have further discussions before January, 1947, to consider the possibility of assessing the prospective requirements of the United Kingdom for 1949 and of negotiating a contract for that year. The new price for bacon means an increase of approximately $3 per hog in price. The order in council of 1944 established a premium of $3 on A's and $2 on B's per hog until six months after the war. The premium is to be decreased by $1 to $2 on A's and $1 on B's per hog. This will provide for a net increase of $2 per hog in price and premium combined.
6.	Cheese. The present contract for the supply of 125 million pounds of cheese to the United Kingdom each year expires on 31st March, 1947. It was agreed that this should be extended to 31st March, 1948, at the same prices. The contract should cover 125 million pounds.
7.	An extension of the contract to cover the season ending 31st March, 1949, has also been agreed with prices to be fixed at a later date, and to this end the United Kingdom and Canadian representatives will review the arrangements before January, 1947.
8.	Evapcftated milk. It was agreed that a contract at current basic prices should be concluded to cover a minimum of 600,000 cases per annum for the two seasons ending 31st March, 1947 and 1948.
9.	Roller dried skim milk powder. It' was agreed that the United Kingdom should purchase 3,000 tons from the 1946 production of roller dried skim milk powder.
10.	Eggs. The United Kingdom desires to obtain increased quantities of Canadian shell eggs during the months from October to April inclusive, and more especially during the months from October to December inclusive. Owing to difficulties in handling supplies in the United Kingdom during the summer months Canada was requested to cease ship-

National Flag
ments of shell eggs by 1st May each year diverting the summer surplus to the production of frozen melange and/or sugar dried eggs.
11.	It was agreed that the current contract which expires on December 31, 1946, should be extended to cover the supply to the United Kingdom of 1,750,000 cases of shell eggs and
5,000	tons of dried eggs in 194/7 at the current basic prices for the shell eggs.
12.	The United Kingdom has agreed to furnish to Canada by the autumn of 1946 (preferably by October) an indication of the requirements of eggs in shell and dried or frozen form during 1948.
13.	Meat. In order to maintain the wartime carcass meat ration, the United Kingdom will require all the beef and mutton which Canada can spare in 1946 and, so far as can be foreseen at present, in 1947 and probably in 1948. It was agreed to continue discussions of the extension of the current contract to cover supplies for 1947.
14.	The United Kingdom will be ready to purchase all the hog casings which Canada can provide up to 1948. Offals and tongues will also be required and these will be the subject of further discussions.
15.	The United Kingdom requested an increase in the export in carcass form of meat suitable for sausage manufacture.

The house resumed from Monday,, March 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fernand Viau for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Bracken, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

Mr. Speaker, I
understand that, according to a well established custom which, as it were, has become a rule of this house, the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne affords to every member an opportunity to state his views on the various problems.
(Text):
Order. I must point out to hon. members that, owing to the noise in the chamber, it is impossible to hear the hon. member who is speaking.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker. I suppose it was because I was speaking in French that my colleagues started to leave the chamber. I submit that it is not only my right but my duty as well, for the first time this session, to address the chair in my own language.

(Translation): It should nevertheless be remembered that on the conclusion of this debate we shall all have to vote.	We
now have before us three motions.	The
first one on which we shall have to vote is the One moved by the honourable member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), leader of the C.C.F. party. I feel that I am not mistaken in saying that, for the first time since I have the honour to sit in this house, we have in that motion a definite and clear statement of the whole doctrine on which is based the policy of that party. The first part of the motion reads as follows:
We respectfully submit, however, that in the opinion of this house, Your Excellency's advisers in their reliance on private enterprise have failed to propose the comprehensive -national planning which the present emergency demands;
That is a blame, a condemnation not about the conduct or the policy of the government, but about the confidence which the government holds toward private enterprise. It is, as I said a few moments ago, a clear and definite statement of the whole doctrine on which that party's policy is based.
I have already had occasion, since I have become a member of this house, to support by my vote and my words many of the reforms advocated by the C.C.F. party, but when it comes to voting on. such a clear-cut statement of principles, I have no hesitation in opposing such a motion, because I still have confidence in the economic system under which we are living, notwithstanding its flaws.
I realize that such a system sometimes gives rise to abuses; however, an administration which is vigilant and conscious of its responsibilities can stamp out such abuses and there is no call to eliminate or overthrow our economic system under the pretext that is not perfect. It would be equivalent to killing a man while trying to cure him. This is why I feel it to be my duty to oppose this amendment by my vote.
Then we will be called upon to vote on the motion of the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Bracken), leader of the Progressive Conservative party. The amendment, considered independently of everything else, contains a condemnation, or rather a censure of the present government, with which I probably could agree because I think most of its grounds are well taken. For instance, in the first paragraph, the administration is blamed for having:
Failed to -meet the needs of veter ans and workers by -planning -reconversion so as to avoid unemployment and dislocation;
When I think that unemployment has already become extensive; when I realize that in Quebec, for example, thousands of persons

The Address-Mr. Dorian
are unable to find jobs, I am inclined to agree with this condemnation of the government's policy.
The fourth assertion of 'this motion is the following:
Failed to relieve the tax burden particularly on low income groups.
As in the case of any motion, it is imperative that not only the wording itself be taken into account, but also the preamble on which the motion has been based. In the speech of the leader of the oppostiion, introducing his motion, I find that he wishes to remove the effects of the evil he mentions, while stating that he approves of the causes of this same evil. Here is a statement I quote from his speech in the house, when he was sipeaking about the loan we are going to grant Great Britain:
These figures total an annual payment exceeding ?50 million for each of -the next few years.
If we intend to reduce taxation and give work to our people, it is impossible, at the same time, to increase the tax burden by the important amount mentioned by the leader of the opposition. In view of the arguments brought out in support of the amendment of which I have just spoken, I do not believe I could logically and fairly vote for that motion.
Indeed, I am not afraid to state, at this moment, that this amendment is nothing but a motion of want of confidence; but I. have no reasons to vote against the present administration, knowing, at the same time, that my vote cannot be interpreted as an approval of the whole government policy.
Mr. Speaker, a third vote will be taken on the main motion, if we are called upon to vote, because it often happens that, the main motion is carried without a recorded vote. Now, rightly or wrongly, but I rather think it is wrongly, a vote in favour of the address in reply to the speech from the throne is sometimes considered as implying approval of all the bills announced in the speech from the throne. I recognize that in the one which we are now considering, ^ there are; projects that should be supported, and there are some with which I, for one, am in complete agreement, as for instance, the redistribution bill which I advocated during the (session held last year, as well as the definition of Canadian citizenship. On the other hand there are other measures which I cannot support. Thus, a paragraph of the speech from the throne reads as follows:
You will also be -asked to make -provision for , the permanent armed forces, to the composition of which much consideration- has been given.
Obviously, we have not yet been informed about the consideration given to that matter. We do not know what is involved. Neither do we know how many soldiers will be included in those permanent forces, or the manner in which it is proposed to maintain them. Consequently, I cannot blindly support that paragraph in the speech from the throne.
There is another paragraph which I cannot endorse. It reads as follows:
At this session yon will be asked to approve an ,agreement recently concluded for a loan to the United Kingdom which will help maintain the British market for Canadian food products and other exports.
Therefore, this endorses the loan we intend to grant to the United Kingdom.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not wish to discuss this matter thoroughly at the present time since it will crop up again during this session.
Hear! Hear!

For the time being, I shall only say that after the war years we have just gone through, our people did not expect such a policy. During the war, it was said that patience was needed and we ourselves, at times, had to explain to our constituents that they must await the end of the armed conflict for various public works which they had long been requesting, because they urgently required them. In view of the situation arising out of the loan, and the obligations it will entail and considering that no important public works are announced, it is greatly to be feared that the projects planned for the past few years will not be carried out.
When I think of the numerous villages in the Charlevoix-Saguenay constituency which are now threatened with complete annihilation by the rising tides of the sea which every year sweep away a further portion of the shore, the danger is so imminent that the next storm might literally wipe these villages off the map. These Canadians, I say, have the right to demand that the government carry out the public works projects needed to protect their property.
Considering also the inadequate means of communication on the North Shore of the St. Lawrence which -make it impossible for the inhabitants of that district to live a decent life,
I claim that these people are fully entitled to' insist that the government spend part of the -public monies on improving their communications system, rather than using that money to pay the interest on loans made by ourselves to other countries. I think of the gallant
The Address-Mr. Dorion

inhabitants of Ile-aux-Coudres who, living some sixty miles from Quebec City, are completely .isolated from the rest of the world for approximately six months every year, because they have no wharves which could be used the year round.
About two years ago a group of citizens of Ile-aux-Coudres tried to cross the river to take a seriously ill man to the hospital, and I remember that they did their utmost in a small boat through floating ice to get him to the mainland where he could have obtained the required medical attention, but the man died because the weather prevented them from reaching the mainland before it was too late. If the people of Ile-aux-Coudires had suitable wharves they could organize a year round ferry service to the mainland.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I contend that before paying millions every year on account of the loan made to another country, our leaders should show the people that they are ready to undertake the public works which are sorely needed.
For that reason I must inform you that should a vote be called on the main motion I would have to vote against it.
There is also another matter about which nearly all those who have taken part in the present debate have spoken; I mean that matter of espionage of which I intend to say a few words.
First of all, I must say that I agree, with all those who have condemned the procedure followed in this case, in that I have deep respect for magna charta, which has been brought out with a view to proving that_ it had been violated by the government in acting the way it did in the arrest of the individuals whose names have now been revealed. However, Mr. Speaker, because I have deep respect and sincere admiration for the magna charta and because I want it to continue to protect our rights and liberties, I contend that the government has acted wisely.
The government acted the way it did in making the arrests precisely to prevent the sabotage of the magna charta. In my opinion the saying, "desperate ills call for desperate remedies," remains true. I am quite sure that the magna charta would have contained clauses pertaining to sabotage and treason had the possibility of such acts been forseseen at the time. Therefore, in view of the situation brought to light by the report of the commissioners, and especially by the inquest under way in Montreal, I contend that nobody Should hesitate to approve the attitude

of the government and particularly that of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Sit. Laurent) in the matter.
When, for instance, I see such items as that published in Saturday Night of March 23, and written by Willes Chitty, I wonder if one can be serious in making such statements. I shall read two sentences of that article.
(Text):
Yet Canada tolerates, with scarce a voice raised in .protest, the sweeping away with a stroke of the pen all the fruits of the struggle of the British peoples for freedom and democracy. . . .
So, perhaps, having said all this very badly, we may sum up our indictment if .as it ought to be-but never will be-laid against the war criminals at home. In our eyes, much as we despise the treason those now charged .and yet to be charged with the contemptible crime of espionage, the crimes committed in the name of freedom by the bureaucrat and .politician are far more heinous.
(Translation):	The publication of such
articles in an important and highly respectable newspaper does not constitute a frank and honest discussion of the important matter at hand. Besides, one could find to-day in our gaols hundreds of individuals who, notwithstanding the protection granted under our laws, and under the magna charta, of which so much has been said, are held in prison before they. have been sentenced, even before they have been accused; everyone knows that any man who is arrested is held in jail until his arraignment before a judge, who decides whether or not to grant bail, and even when the latter is granted, it very often happens that the required amount of cash cannot be raised and handed to the cler kof the court, in which case the man must remain in prison for weeks and even months. Very often the man is acquitted because the evidence is insufficient and does not warrant a trial.
If the principle invoked to blame the government and accuse them of having transgressed the provision of the magna charta were carried to its extreme-which seems to have been the desire of some people in the past few days-such cases of detention would no longer be possible and' no one could be kept in jail under circumstances such as those I have mentioned.
That is why, I believe, such an unjustified storm was raised. I was very much surprised to hear those who had no right to protest voice the strongest objections.
I remember very well that last fall, when the government presented a motion-bill 15, it Was-to extend the War Measures Act, some hon. members were opposed to granting such wide powers .to the government; and

The Address-Mr. Dorion
everyone recalls also how my motion to have the bill set aside could not be voted on for lack of support.
Is the government to be blamed if, having secured the necessary powers to enact P.C. 6444 of October 6, 1945, they invoked those very powers to act as they have done in this spy probe?
Mr. Speaker, if the government and more particular!}' the Minister of Justice are to be commended for the way they have dealt with .this matter, we must not forget that our present difficulties are nevertheless due to neglect on the part of the government,
I cannot but recall the obvious sympathy which has existed in recent years between the liberal party and the communist party in Canada.
That is not so good.

I remember that after the 1935 elections, when the liberal party was returned to power, one of its first steps was to repeal section 98 of the Criminal Code. Perhaps that section did not constitute a sure means of preventing what is happening to-day but surely it was a serious obstacle to the dissemination of communistic propaganda. I remember also that in 1937-1938 the Quebec provincial government, then led by the hon. Maurice Duplessis, had the Padlock Act passed by the Legislative Assembly. How vehemently have the members of the liberal party protested against that law. It was claimed then that the Hon. Maurice Duplessis was acting like a dictator. And yet, Mr. Speaker, it was another means of preventing the dissemination of subversive and communist ideas.
Did it succeed in preventing it?

This marked sympathy between the liberal and communist parties became even more pronounced during the last general election. In a review published by the communist party, in July, 1944, there was an article by Fred Rose, the hon. member for Cartier, from which I quote the following:
Ten days ago, Tim Ruck, national leader of the Labor-Progressive party, submitted to the *labour 'movement and to the country a project for the coalition of liberal, agricultural and labour forces, with a view to solving essential national problems.
And a little further:
I .have supported the speech from the throne outlining the programme of the King government for 1944. It definitely implied the adherence of Canada to the Teheran agreements, and announced a comprehensive programme of social reforms and plans for the post-war period. In regard to all major questions, that speech met practically all the requirements and immediate aims of the labour movement. It behooves the labour movement to cooperate with the liberals and with all patriotic forces in the struggle for the implementation of those plans. During the debate I advocated a union of all liberal and labour forces, to form the nucleus of national unity, to hasten the implementation of the plans submitted 'and to ensure their fulfilment.
Was this agreement approved by the liberal party?

I say to the hon. member for Labelle that I know that one day the communist party offered to cooperate with the C.C.F. party, but the latter immediately rejected the offer. I have never heard that the leaders of the liberal party had rejected such an offer of cooperation by the communist party.

The right hon. the Prime
Minister has done so.

Mr. Speaker, not only have the government displayed this measure of sympathy which I have mentioned, but through their negligence and their laisser faire attitudes, they have allowed the dissemination of communist ideas.
There was the Padlock Act to prevent that.

There was the Padlock Act, but if it was not applied by the Attorney General of the province, it is because, in 1939, the Liberal party was in power. It is probably the reason why the Act was not enforced.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, this laisser faire attitude was favourable to the steady dissemination of communist ideologies. I recall, for instance, that after the death of Louis Francoeur, a commentator of the C.B.C. on the French network, and a respectable man who enjoyed the esteem of his fellow-citizens, on several occasions his successors have expressed views echoing the communistic doctrine and they had thus instilled that communist poison, into our homes. Although some prominent men have called the attention of the authorities to the unabated campaign of propoganda carried on by communists, the government did not deem it proper to take action.
I have here Le Droit of May 31, 1944, and I find the following on the first page:
The Communists Are Very Active in Canada, says Mr. Kirkconmdl
Montreal, May 30 (CP).-Mr. Watson Kirk-connell, of Hamilton, Ont., stated yesterday before the annual meeting of the Royal Society of Canada, held at the University of Montreal, that "in so far as the communists in Canada
The Address-Mr. Dorion

are concerned, the dissolution of the Comintern has been followed by an unparalleled renewal of activity.
"Instead of calmly disbanding, he said, the Communist party, under its new name of Labor-progressive, has launched a campaign in its own country."
It is clearly demonstrated today.
A violent Marx-Lenin propaganda campaign is flooding Canada at the present time, he said.
Although the Labor-progressive party, whose national leader is Tim Buck, of Toronto, publicly professes to be on good terms with capitalism and although it dares blame the C.C.F. for its socialist tendencies, at the same time, it distributes revolutionary literature all through Canada, said Mr. Kdrkconnell.
What about the padlock legislation of Hon. Maurice Duplessis?

There is more, Mr. Speaker. Not only has the present government allowed this propaganda, but I claim that they have even encouraged it by certain, official publications. Here is one entitled Chronique ouvriere, French, and The Labour Facts, in English, and the preamble of the first number, dated February 15, 1944, states very plainly what it is all about:
Monthly information service on .the part played by labour in the war effort, supplied to the Canadian labour press by the Wartime Information Board, Ottawa.
This is indeed a government organization.
AH the following .information may be copied or reprinted according to the needs of the various newspapers.
This first number of February 14, 1944, contains the following:
Canadian-Soviet Exchange of Labour Information
All the 'Canadian labour unions earnestly welcome the suggestion of the labour representatives at the national council for Canadian-Soviet friendship, who have proposed an exchange of questions and answers between the labour unions of both countries. The project has been approved by both the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada and the Canadian Trade-Congress.
And a little farther on:
Representative groups are organizing local committees in a certain number of communities. Through the national council and these local committees, the labour unions may obtain Soviet films and photos illustrating scenes of current life .in the 'Soviet union, posters displayed in factories, books and .publications on various aspects of Soviet activities.
This is quoted from a federal government official publication of February, 1944. From another issue, dated June 15, 1944, I quote the following excerpt:
( USSR Workers Learn More About The Canadian War Effort
The workers of the USSR are getting a better perspective of the Canadian labour movement and the part it plays in the current war.

Through the national council for Canadian-Soviet friendship, organized with the object of promoting better relations between the two countries, the Canadian labour unions are entering directly in relation with the corresponding unions in the USSR.
And again:
Besides organizing this exchange of communications between the labour movements in both countries, the national council supplies the unions of our country with authorized speakers, films, photos and literature on the Soviet union.
This again is to be found in a federal government official publication.
I therefore contend, Mr. Speaker, that the government is responsible for the situation with which we are faced nowadays; to my mind, the government, in order to satisfy the current demands of our people, will have to go further than the inquiry now in progress and will have to do more than prosecute only a few individuals. A thorough investigation into the various departments of the federal administration is imperative, since it is obvious that the ramifications of the organization brought to light recently are far more widespread than those which have been uncovered so far. The people will be satisfied with nothing less than a comprehensive investigation which will make it possible for the government to sweep away everything which smacks of communism and communistic propaganda. I am confident that after such a clean-up, and I hope the present government will perform the task thoroughly, life in our country will once again be worth living.

HE ON (Argenteuil): Mr. Speaker, following a commendable custom, I wish to use his mother tongue, for which he no doubt holds a deep attachment, to congratulate the honourable member for St. Boniface (Mr. Viau) for the fluent delivery and the clearness of expression with which he has moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Hear. hear.

My honourable friend has had the thoughtfulness of expressing to his compatriots from Quebec the gratitude of our western brothers for the help given to the western French radio station. For the present, I shall merely emphasize that old Quebec, which ever "remembers", is not unaware of the true situation in which our French-speaking compatriots from other provinces find themselves, and that, in the

The Address-Mr. Heon
words of the old ballad "It always thinks of it and never forgets". Finally, and this will be my last word on this subject, so long as our compatriots can rely on the enlightened patriotism of distinguished men, and I may mention such names as Baudoux, Yelle, d'Eschambault, Beauchemin, de Margerie, Joyal, Denis, Paimchaud, Lacerte, Bernier, Beaubien, Marcoux and many others, there will be every reason to hope and rejoice.
(Text):
I fully subscribe, Mr. Speaker, to the traditional congratulations heaped upon the mover (Mr. Yiau) and the seconder (Mr. Winters) of the address for the able and dignified way in which they acquitted themselves of their not inconsiderable task. The leaders of the various groups in this house must also be complimented upon the distinction and ability with which they discussed, and in some cases refrained from discussing, the grave issues and problems mentioned in the speech from the throne and with which this house must of necessity be confronted during the present session.
The speech from the throne reveals a sad truth in the following excerpt:
The turmoil which has followed in the wake of war has created new problems for governments in all parts of the globe. The world is full of unrest. Hunger, privation and suffering have become the lot of millions.
To all the peoples of occupied countries who during the war listened, often at the risk of death, at their secret radios to our pledge that if they would believe in the righteousness of our cause and help us defeat the common foe, "all the men in all the lands would live out their lives in freedom from fear and want," these enunciations of fact are far from encouraging. Yet it cannot be otherwise. For six anguished years the nations of the world have literally drenched the earth with blood, drained their resources and reserves to the last ounce, sacrificed the finest of their youth, destroyed their places of worship, their institutions of learning, their hospitals, their museums, their manufactures and their crops. The supreme cruelty lies in the fact that those least responsible for such a shameful condition in the affairs of men, the women and children of these destitute lands, will suffer the most and pay the highest price. They may well ask themselves, as we all should, if that is really what our much-vaunted Christian civilization has brought us to, twenty centuries after the Sermon on the Mount.
Shall we, as after the first world war, remain drunk with the wine of victory, return to our egoistical complacencies and forget the price
paid, or shall we restore and permanently reestablish throughout a terrified world those tenets of the Christian doctrine without which an enduring peace can never be signed, much less adhered to?
The answer lies with every one of us, and on this answer will depend whether we practice-and whether the oppressed nations will believe that we practise-what we preach when we say we are the champions of Christianity and freedom; or whether we have been and are prostituting these words to achieve our own selfish ends.
The masses of Poland, the Baltic states, the Balkans, Indonesia, India, Egypt, China and Iran must not be allowed to believe that the war has been fought for the supremacy [DOT] of one of five imperialisms, or for the securing of "sanitary cordons" between one great power and another, or for oil for the lamps of the Kremlin, or for battleships, nor for the privilege of making cannons instead of butter, or for the liberty of spreading anti-Christian and totalitarian ideologies, or for creating powerful fifth columns, but solely for the maintenance of moral principles, liberty and decency in every part of the world.
We have been assured that Canada has emerged from the war with its international prestige greatly enhanced, and it is apparent that through our proposed commitments we have taken a deep plunge in international affairs. I am one of those who believe in truth, simplicity and frankness in the realm of external affairs. Our policy should, in the words of the distinguished internationalist Harold Nicholson, be as follows:
Leaders in democratic countries should by 'all mean9 in their power refrain from policies which are difficult to explain openly and in detail. The public understands principles, whereas it does not understand manoeuvres: and a foreign policy based upon ascertainable and lavowable principles is more likely to recommend the ordinary citizen's consent, than one based in any respect upon ingenuity and adventure.
This citation should be given a place of honour in all the foreign offices of the united nations, particularly the big three, and more particularly among the Big Three in the following order, in view of its importance to themselves and the immediate necessity of allaying growing fear and distrust in their ulterior motives: the Bear, the Lion and the Eagle.
Peter Howard, the eminent author, has admirably defined the only foreign policy which can honestly and permanently be adopted by
the Big Three, if world peace is to become something more than a pipe dream:
The great powers must educate themselves to the conception that ther duty is to serve mankind rather than dominate it.
i
The Address-Mr. Heon

A newspaper clipping sent to me by a friend at Harvard, whose authorship I cannot establish, puts the question brutally but thoroughly thus:
We don't need pious, well-meant preachments which only confuse further the present confusion. We want an honest, clear-cut answer to the question:	On what grounds should permissions
he allowed 'to others which we denied to Hitler? Efficient, working agreements must :be reached . . . but on what terms? And at what price?
We are dead against robbery, rape and murder whether by the Wehrmacht or by others. We condemn brutal absorption of small, helpless nations by Hitler or by anyone else.
Hence, Mr. Speaker, since Wendell Willkie's "One World" has come to be, since the atomic age is with us, Canada must play its part in world affairs, a part commensurate with its immediate means and essential needs, and within the margin of its own domestic security and welfare. As much as we must, through Christian charity, our duty to humanity, and self-protection, render help to others, we also have to discharge our duties towards our fel-low-Canadians. There is a limit past which a nation of 12,000,000 people, boasting a national debt of $16 billion which must continue to increase with our contemplated commitments, cannot go. We must remember that a Canada whose citizens would be saddled with a backbreaking national debt, and ever-increasing taxes, thereby becoming discontented, would be a direct liability to the United Nations, and could not therefore render the help and services which are now pledged and expected from it. As compared with our good neighbour to the south, who is one of the Big Three, and apparently the biggest of them, we have undertaken a tremendous burden of international financing and obligations: on the proposed loan to Britain we are 3-5 times more generous than the United States of America. If the great republic wants to equal our contribution in ratio of population and dollar for dollar, it should lend $12,260 million without interest. For our friends to the south of us, who love to establish world records, this is one to shoot at! ! !
Apropos of the British loan, Mr. Speaker, I must candidly admit that I have not found amongst my constituents, nor in my province, and particularly amongst the farming and lower-income groups, that degree of enthusiasm which has become evident in certain quarters. To these of my fellow citizens who are not acquainted with the intricacies of cyclical financing, international obligations, and world responsibilities, and who are mainly concerned with making both ends meet in their own little family budget after income taxes have been computed and deducted, the 
proposed loan is more than a question mark.
I believe that on this proposed loan, as in any other important item of the country's policy, particularly foreign policy, the government should take this House and the country into its confidence. It is not the privilege of the rank-and-file Canadian to have access to the secret files of the ministry of External Affairs or the ministry of finance, nor has he the time or the training to study the curvaceous trends of international intrigues or politics. The popular saying, "no taxation without representation" should be extended to "no taxation without explanation", so that every Canadian will know in advance what is expected of him and will then be free to determine where his true course lies.
Perhaps if Canadians were told the true situation in Great Britain, its appalling financial position, its declining world trade, and the importance of maintaining, within the European sphere, sympathy and goodwill, the answer might be quite different. Why not put the cards on the table? Marshal Stalin has, without any scruples, in his answer to Mr. Churchill's speech. Mr. Bevin has, in answer to Vishinsky's accusation. Let that be the rule the whole way through!
Personally, and I owe it to my constituents, I am awaiting the explanation of the sponsor of the British loan bill before I form a definite opinion. I want to be shown that this loan will be to the best interests of Canada and world peace, that it will help convince the majority of the nations of Europe that they must choose between democracy and another regime, and that it will provide markets for our products and furnish work and wages to Canadians. But by all means let us have the truth, the whole truth, on this measure. Canadians love truth, but they hate half truths and deliberate lies.
On this proposed loan, I should like to quote an excerpt from an article by Henry Clay in the April 1946 issue of Foreign Affairs:
The problem is the long-term problem which will still face the United Kingdom when the transition from war to peace has been completed-the problem of establishing a balance in external relations. The proposed loan itself is likely to be exhausted before the transition is complete, but .the conditions attached to it will continue to have effect. By ruling out any policy of tying exports with imports bilaterally they will deprive British exports of a certain support they enjoyed in. the thirties. Taken with article eight, section four of the Bretton Woods agreement, .they subject British monetary policy once more to the requirements of convertibility which will compel a prompter balancing of imports than was necessary when sterling was inconvertible.

The Address-Mr. Heon
On- the w-h-ole, then, the -effect of the 'agreement is more to postpone than .to ease this long-term problem of Britain's.
In all of these international issues one very important principle must not be forgotten: Canada is not in a more advantageous but rather a less disadvantageous situation than some other countries. It is a fact that we have not been invaded, nor have we been stamped with the immediate horrors of war. This is wholly due to the grace of God, our geographical situation, the valour of our arms, and the (scientific certainty that planes must sacrifice distance to bomb loads. If we had been geographically situated where Poland is, who is there in the house to say that an eagle would not have struck us in the breast and a bear in the back? Let us not lose the sense of real perspective. We are not as badly off as some other nations; that is self-evident, and thank God for it: our territory has not been riddled, nor have our women and children known the fear of a heeled and ruthless enemy knocking at the front door. Thank God for thatl We are not in the humiliating and demoralizing position of having to count on the generosity of other peoples for food, clothing or credits, nor are we, through immediate exigencies and physical needs, unfortunately forced to forget national pride and international prestige. Thank God for that!
But all these situations do not make our own position one whit better than it really is. Our war veterans full and successful rehabilitation is not yet achieved, and one has only to visit, as I do, the various branches of our veterans' associations to realize that. Our housing problem remains unsolved; one has only to visit any city or town in Canada to become convinced of that. Unemployment is too high for comfort, and it is not a feature of our economy that we can truly boast of. Our industrial reconversion from war to peace lags, and one has only to enter any store to find out the discouraging shortage of consumer goods. Finally, let one glance at the income tax schedules, and he will readily grasp what our financial burdens are. It is not unfair to say, then, that although we are not as badly off as some other countries, we still have plenty to do to improve our own situation, and the Canadian people will expect us to do so immediately.
Another great issue is occupying the minds of our people through the shocking revelations of the Taschereau-Kellock commission. Personally I feel that too much wrongful publicity is being given to the affair and to those involved. There has been such an orgy of pictures of the accused, portrayed in delightful and affectionate poses with their wives, 63260-18
that one would almost be led to think that some of the accused have hired Hollywood press agents. There is a grave danger that the ends of justice may not be served; and those of us here in the legal profession will easily understand what I have in mind. The -accused have not yet been tried, and the twelve men who will decide their fate remain to be selected. With this flood of publicity it will not be easy to select jurymen who have not formed an opinion, and the defence will have -an opportunity of challenging almost everyone on the jury panel. Further, the accused have not yet been found guilty, and my years of experience as Crown prosecutor have taught me- to expect the unexpected verdict from the twelve "tried and true" men. With the flowing headlines and imaginative stories that are being circulated, the accused who may be acquitted will proclaim themselves martyrs to the cause of the proletariat, whilst those who may be found guilty will loudly proclaim that they were the victims of prejudice and persecution. Some restraint is in order; once the verdict is rendered, there will be time to come to conclusions and- tell the Canadian people all that should be told on this highly disturbing matter.
If I may have your indulgence, Mr. Speaker,
I -would like to close by giving briefly my opinion on the contentious question of a Canadian flag. The various polls conducted amongst all sections of our people, and particularly our armed forces, have shown that an absolute majority deems it a matter of national pride that Canada should have a flag which it can truly call its own. The difficulty arises however in the choice of a proper, logical and true design, and the various sections of our people have expressed widely-divergent views. Some have shed abundant tears over the prospect that the union jack might be withdrawn from the design; others have championed the cause of the fleur-de-lis, but almost all have shown a particular in'clination for the maple leaf.
I humbly submit that our true status within the Commonwealth suggests an honourable and satisfactory compromise. It is not the union jack which binds the peoples of the Commonwealth together, much less the fleur-de-lis. It is the allegiance to a common and revered crown which has given unity and strength through peace and war. It is our loyalty to the crown which has inspired us to take up arms and fight the good fight. Let it again be the crown that will bind alll Canadians, of whatever origin they may be, together under a flag for which they will be proud to live, work and die. The most rabid nationalist

The Address-Mr. Bracken

and the most fervent imperialist alike will proclaim their allegiance to the king of Canada.
I am not versed in heraldics, but I feel that a flag of sober colouring with a proud and large maple leaf in the middle, in the centre of which would be imprinted a large and distinctive crown, would meet with universal respect and approval.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
A week or more ago I spoke in this house and at the conclusion of my remarks moved an amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In that amendment, among other things, I criticized the agricultural policy of the government. A day or two later the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) spoke for the government and discussed some of the suggestions I had made; and
he stated the f...sent policy of the government.
In the midst ot his remarks he made one statement which indicated that I was taking a different view now, being a politician, from that which I had taken some years ago when I did not suffer from the disadvantages of that classification; and he indicated further that I was correct in the earlier days but that being in my present position, I am wrong now. In view of these statements, and in view of the importance of agricultural production in these days in Canada, as well as in the world. I felt it my duty to take up some of the time of the house this afternoon to deal with this particular matter.
My amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, among other things, declared that the government had "failed to adjust their agricultural production plans to meet the altered conditions of the world's demands." In that address I said:
The wheat acreage of western Canada can be increased by nearly four million acres by going back to the percentage of summer-fallow that was used prior to the time we started paying people not to grow wheat. We do not need to reduce the acreage that is being used for feed crops for animals.
In what I shall say this afternoon I shall deal chiefly with wheat, because under these circumstances it is of major importance in the world's food economy. I shall touch briefly on dairy products, and even more briefly say a word about the general position of agriculture in the Canadian economy.
Further on in that address I said:
The acreage in fallow under pre-war conditions would be about fifteen or sixteen million. By going back to that amount of summer-fallow we can get three or four million acres more on which to grow wheat, which would give us thirty or forty million bushels; and in this way we will do much more to help correct famine

conditions in Britain or somewhere else than will be accomplished by all the effort to save food-though I am not discouraging the government in that policy.
And I added this:
Wheat farmers need to be allowed to get more of the world price if they are to seed three or four million acres of this land which will otherwise lie fallow this year, if they are to decrease the amount of fallow land from 19-4 million acres to about 16 million acres. All they have to do is, instead of summer-fallowing a hundred acres, to summer-fallow eighty and use the other twenty for crop.
The Minister of Agriculture has taken issue with this position. He defends the governments' policy of encouraging the summerfallowing of some twenty million acres out of sixty or sixty-one million acres now under cultivation for cereal crops in western Canada, as contrasted with the use of a little less than sixteen millions for this purpose before the war. That is the general position.
To those not familiar with the practice of summer-fallowing, let me say that it is a practice that is developed for the conservation of moisture in farming areas with low rainfall. In western Canada last year, and for a few years previously, nearly twenty million out of approximately sixty million acres under cultivation for cereal crops in those three prairie lay fallow for the purpose of conserving moisture.
I wonder if the members of the house appreciate the extent of territory twenty million acres represents? I have here figures for the total improved farm acreage in each of the provinces of Canada. The nearly twenty million acres lying idle out there represent twenty-six times the total improved farm acreage in Prince Edward Island, .twenty-four times the total improved farm acreage in Nova Scotia, sixteen times the total improved farm acreage in New Brunswick, twice the improved farm acreage of Quebec, fifty per cent more than the improved farm acreage of Ontario, twice as much as in Manitoba, over half as much as the improved total acreage in Saskatchewan, nearly as much as the total improved acreage in Alberta, and more than twenty times the total improved farm acreage in British Columbia.
I give these comparisons to show the extent of the territory which now lies idle. The question before this parliament and the Canadian people is whether it is wise to continue that proportion of land now lying idle when the world needs cereals for food, or whether it would not be wiser to reduce it to the neighbourhood of sixteen million acres; in other words, to summer-fallow four acres or a little more where we formerly summer-fallowed five.

The Address-Mr. Bracken
In defending the government's position the Minister of Agriculture charged me with having one set of views on matters of agricultural policy when I was supposed to be an expert in that field, and another set of views now that I have become, to use his term, "a politician". He made clear that the views I formerly held were sound, and that the government, of which he is a member, was now following them in so far as this particular aspect of agriculture is concerned. He sought to leave with the house the impression that, being a politician, I had departed from my earlier sound views and that what I had to say now on this issue was not to be taken seriously.
I am speaking to this house to-day for two reasons. First, I want to answer the wholly unfounded charge that, as an agriculturist, I spoke one way in earlier days, and that now, being a politician, I speak another way. Second, I think it necessary in the nation's interest to expose the fallacies of some of the government's agricultural policies, particularly those with respect to wheat and dairy products. In doing this, I shall analyse the minister's address, answer his baseless charges with his own words, and show from the reports of his own department and the records of the government's bureau of statistics that his policy deserves censure and not commendation at this time, and that it should be altered to help meet the present emergency.
The minister in his address, apart from the several side issues he brought in, attempted to do three main things.
(1)	He attempted to discredit the proposal I advanced that, in this time of food crisis, the summer-fallow acreage of western Canada might be safely reduced from 19,400,000 acres to about 15,800,000, and that an additional
3,600,000	acres be thus made available for seeding to wheat-an additional acreage five times the total of the improved land in the Province of Prince Edward Island. He represented this suggestion as being the view of "a politician" and that it differed from the views I held as an agriculturist in earlier days.
(2)	The minister attempted to show that the increased production of farm products since 1940 was due to the government's policy of increasing the percentage of summer-fallow from about twenty-eight per cent shortly before the war to some thirty-three per cent in the years following 1940. To put it another way, he was critical of and rejected the suggestion that the acreage of bare summer-fallow in western Canada should in this emergency be reduced from the 19,400,000
63260-18i
acres proposed by the government to something less than 16,000,000 acres, or to be more specific, 15,800,000 acres. He saw no virtue in adding, say 3,600,000 acres that would thus be made available to the limited objective of 23,400,000 odd acres suggested by the government for wheat for this year.
(3)	The minister's third main point was that the government In 1943 switched its policy from one of encouraging live stock production 'to one of encouraging a greater production of wheat. To use his own words:
We did not wait until everyone over in Europe was shouting for more food before we changed our policy from one of encouraging the intensive production of meat and dairy products to one of increasing the production of wheat.
I propose to deal with these three main points the minister sought to establish. I shall deal also with several other misleading and incorrect statements he made. And I shall conclude my remarks with some general observations on the relationship of agriculture to the general economy of this country.
Let me deal first very briefly with the minister's main points. He attempted to throw discredit upon- me by representing that I preached one agricultural doctrine thirty years ago and that I preach another now. In this connection I propose to show that he misquoted what I said in 1916 by omitting essential parts of what I did say. I am not saying that the minister did1 it deliberately; I am quite sure he would not do that. I shall show that what I said in those early years, and which the minister applauded as being sound practice for the farmers in the west, is exactly the same view I advance to-day, a view which he now says is both unwise and "political."
In connection with the minister's second main point, namely, that the government's policy of maintaining a higher than normal acreage of summer-fallow will increase the total production of wheat and other cereals, I shall show (1) that the policy of the government in this respect is not one that will increase total production but rather will decrease it; (2) that reducing the acreage of crops sown and increasing the acreage of land left summer-fallow beyond the percentage of pre-war days is a policy of decreasing production and not one of increasing production.
As for the minister's third main point, namely, that the government changed its views in 1943 from encouraging live stock production to encouraging wheat production, I shall show that the government's policies in this respect have been quite the opposite to what the minister now says they have been. I shall show that the recommendations of his own department similarly disprove his present contention.
The Address-Mr. Bracken

I come now to the second major point the Minister of Agriculture has sought to establish, namely, that by summer-fallowing 19-4 million acres out of 61 millions now under cultivation in western Canada, a larger production will be secured than if only, say,
15.800.000	acres were summer-fallowed. To put it another way, his contention is that with
41.500.000	acres in crop and 19,400,000 not in crop, (summer-fallow), there will be a greater production than if 45,100,000 acres are in crop and only 15,800,000 not in crop.
That is the problem the Canadian farmer is facing. That is the problem we face here in deciding what attitude we shall take with respect to encouraging them in their production plans.
As evidence in support of his theory, the minister referred to the average production of wheat in the years 1935 to 1939 when the percentage of land in fallow in the prairie provinces was about 28J per cent, and compared it with the production in the years 1940 and 1944 when the average in fallow was about 32J per cent. To use the minister's words:
The result was this-referring to wheat.
-the average crop from 1935 to 1939 was 312,000,000 bushels and the average from 1940 to 1944 was 420,000,000 bushels.
That is his argument. He says, Let us summer-fallow more than before the war; let us leave more land idle-even under these critical conditions. A little further down he said:
I am suggesting that we did follow that policy of greatly increasing summer-fallowing and we got the best results we have had in the whole history of Saskatchewan.
In other words, the minister gives all credit for this increased production to the fact that in the latter period there were over 19 million acres per year in summer-fallow and a little less than 22 millions in wheat, whereas in the earlier period there were four million acres less in summer-fallow and about three million acres more in wheat. My answer is that there is no justification whatever for accepting such a theory on the evidence given. The fact is that in the more productive period of 1940-44 there was not only slightly more fallowed land and slightly less cropped land, but there was more favourable weather, there was no major attack from wheat rust, no extensive losses from insects such as grasshoppers and cut-worms, and the varieties of wheat grown were more productive than those available in the preceding period.

Let me give some details. In the 1935-39 period the rainfall averaged 16 per cent less than in the later period. In two years, 1936 and 1937, the sum of the rainfall in the two growing seasons was an inch less than in the one growing season of 1942. One year 1937 was the driest year ever known in the histoiy of the west. In that year I believe Saskatchewan averaged only 2^ bushels of wheat, and large areas produced nothing. Considerable areas, even under summer-fallow, produced nothing. In two years of the 1935-39 period there was a rust epidemic which reduced the production by 160,000,000 bushels; in two years there was serious damage from cut-worms and other insects-grasshoppers, wire worms and saw fly causing a reduction of over 200,000,000 bushels. In one year, 1937, in July, the temperature reached 113 degrees in the shade, an almost all-time record for the prairie region. Whenever the temperature exceeds 100 degrees in the shade for any length of time, out there it means serious consequences to the wheat crop.
In 1942, on the other hand, the yield of wheat was more than three times the yield of 1937, and two and a half times the yield of 1936.
The fault with the minister is that he tabes a given position, and then seeks superficial evidence to bolster it up. In this case he gives ne credit whatever to nature. He takes it all unto himself and to the government, for no other reason than that in one period heavier yields were obtained than in another. I have never before from the lips of any responsible minister heard such a nervy attempt to take unto himself and the government all credit for the weather, and for the relative absence of unfavourable conditions.
The simple fact is that the average yield of wheat in western Canada over a period of years practically always exceeds fifty per cent of the yield of wheat sown on summer-fallow. This means that in all the wheat-growing region of Canada, outside very limited areas where the fifty-fifty plan of fallow and wheat is advisable, the total production will be increased in those rotation systems which crop two-thirds of the land each year or three-quarters of the land each year rather than in those which crop only one-half of it each year.
This does not mean that it is always less economical to follow the two-year fallow system. There are some very dry areas where this should never be departed from even in an emergency, and there are other areas where it may be more economical than any longer rotation; but the fact remains that on the average of the areas where wheat is now

The Address-Mr. Bracken
grown a greater total yield per farm is obtained where the land is cropped two years out of three, or three out of four, than where it is cropped only one year out of two.
All the facts of science and experimental tests go to indicate that the total production would have been considerably greater during the 1940-1944 period than it was had 25,000,000 acres a year been sown rather than the 22,000,000 that were sown.
To further bolster up his contention, the minister instances also the greater yield of oats and barley in the 1940-1944 period as compared with the 1935-1939 period. What he does not tell us here also is that the rainfall was less in the earlier period, that the acreage was less, that the damage form disease and insects was greater, and that nearly all of the oats and barley was grown, not on fallowed land, but on second, third and fourth crop land.
To climax his argument the minister says:
If we had had the increase only in grain production it could be argued that by that policy you do not get more food than by following the other policy.
He supplements this statement by asserting that larger deliveries of hogs were made, more cattle were shipped, and more eggs and dairy products produced. Why he should advance this as an argument to bolster up his case seems incomprehensible. With 6,000,000 acres more of crop land in use in the war period, what other result could have been expected? With better pasturage from increased rains, a bigger acreage of feed crops, and the use even of wheat for live stock consumption, no other result could possibly have been expected.
The minister then follows with the ridiculous argument that this live stock production is an "addition" to these enormous amounts of grain. The obvious fact is that we do not have a double gain when we have large amounts of feed grains and a large live stock production. We can have either one or the other, but not both. Feed grains are consumed where live stock is produced. That is the price we pay for live stock. Obviously, when the acreage sown to feed grains and the acreage used for pasture and hay are all increased, the live stock must necessarily also be increased.
The minister says that by greatly increasing summer-fallow in 1940-1944, he got the best results that had ever been obtained in the whole history of Saskatchewan. The reason he gives for those good results I have shown to be erroneous.
There was another period in the history of the west when equally good acreage yields and better total results were obtained and the summer-fallow land was not then thirtythree per cent but only a little more than twenty-two per cent. It was in the period 1924-1928. In that period the seasonal rainfall was almost one-half inch less than in the 1940-1944 period. In the period, 19241928 wheat in the prairie provinces averaged 18-7 bushels per acre, as compared with 18-9 bushels in the 1940-1944 period. Oats yielded 3T5 bushels as compared with 33-8 bushels; barley, 26-8 bushels as compared with 26-8 bushels; rye, 16-7 bushels as compared with 13-9 bushels, and flax, 8-6 bushels as compared with 7-4 bushels. Yet in that period, 1924-1928, the area of summer-fallow was only 22J per cent as compared with 32J per cent in the later period. Had the lower summer-fallow percentage of the 19241928 period been'used in the 1940-1944 period with its heavier rainfall, the total production in the later period, large as it was, would have been increased by whatever amount the five or six million extra acres would have yielded-an amount of approximately 50,000,000 bushels a year.

The Address-Mr. Bracken

increase the price-nr take his controls off wheat and allow the world price-or let him tell the farmers definitely that they will not in later years be allowed any higher price than he is allowing then to receive to-day. I wish now to refer briefly to the dairy situation, to which I also made reference the other day. About three years ago the government established subsidies for dairy products, which subsidies have remained substantially fixed ever since except for seasonal changes. Yet during the period when dairy returns \vere relatively fixed, dairy farmers' costs have been steadily rising. In western Canada feed costs have risen some forty per cent and farm wages have gone up fifty per cent. In eastern Canada feed prices, since December, 1942, have risen eleven per cent and farm wages have risen twenty-five per cent or more. Good farm labour is difficult to hire, and the result is that dairy production all along the line is decreasing rapidly. The turn came eighteen months ago, in the prairie region, when milk production started to decline. In this area the decline has been going on for eighteen months with no sign of a let-up. In eastern Canada the decline started six months ago and is gaining momentum. All lines of dairy production are falling-cheese, butter and concentrated milk products-and at the same time that production is falling the demand is increasing.
We now have 600,000 more people in Canada than a year ago. At the end of this year there will be another 200,000 more people in Canada than at present. Yet the government sits placidly by and does not seem to realize that price determines production. There is only one way to prevent'the decline in dairy production from developing into a real crisis in the next twelve months, and that is to increase the return to dairy producers now.
The government has taken upon itself the functions of the free-price market. It controls the financial returns to producers through subsidies and price ceilings. If the decline in production is to be stemmed and turned into increasing production, the dairy 
farmers must have higher returns. The

Cana-

They urged that Canada take a leading part in establishing a post-war world policy and asked the dominion government to call upon the nations of the world to organize the united nations organization into a supranational government, first to establish world law; second, to maintain peace; third to administer justice in accordance with world law, and, fourth, that a world government be democratically elected by powers great and small upon an equitable basis. I think this is a time in the world's history when we have to use understanding and exercise patience and1 tolerance. I am not here to defend everything that has been done by the Soviet Union or everything that has been done by any government, but I do ask the members of this house to consider the twenty-five years of misunderstandings that we went through after the last war and the lies and misinformation and propaganda that were given to the people in this and other countries. The post-war economic pattern from England to the Soviet borders is clear. The trend is toward nationalization of key points in the economy. In Britain the Labour party was elected on a platform whose main planks *were the nationalization of the Bank of England, coal, iron and steel, electricity, gas, railways, aviation and all internal transport, with a national board to control investments. In France the parties who won three-fourths of the seats in the national assembly campaigned on a very similar programme, part of which has already been fulfilled in laws covering the Bank of France and other large financial institutions. In Czechoslovakia all four political parties compaigned. for nationalization of mines, heavy industry, electric power, banks and insurance companies, and this programme is rapidly being put into effect. In the United States and in Canada the period of state capitalism has clearly arrived, despite all the claims of economists and advertising psychologists whom big business hires to put science in chains for profit. The capitalist economy has never, since the early pioneer stages, operated without state aid. In the United States and in Canada, it owes its privilege and its power to incorporation rights, the tariffs, the franchises, the subsidies and the state's promotion of foreign trade and investments.
When the second world war burst upon us the production we needed in this country was too great for our big business to handle. The state had in many instances to take over the functions of the capitalist, providing the funds and markets, building plants, securing and allocating raw materials* labour supplies and so on. The highest production records in our history, which big business now claims for so-called private enterprise, were made only with the aid and under the direction of the state.
Even in the international sphere it is clear that our miscalled free enterprise can neither function nor manage our share of the inter- _ national economic arrangements so sadly needed and now, to some extent, being planned. Our proposed loan to Britain, the international monetary fund, the world bank, the social and economic council of UNO, all tell the same story, the necessity for governments to make financial arrangements and the international development of state capitalism in every form. Not all the free enterprise propaganda can conceal the fact that we are moving steadily, in both the international and the national spheres, into the period known historically as state capitalism.
The immediate cause of the European trend toward nationalization is the fact that the

defeat of the nazis has left Europe in economic chaos. Industrial plants have to be rebuilt, and private capital is absolutely unable to tackle the job. Those who have gone through fascist tyranny are not in a frame of mind to rebuild the power of financiers who helped Hitler to office or profited by his system; unable to accept, let alone put into effect, complete socialization. The only way at present to relieve their distress is through limited nationalization methods, or in other words, a state capitalist economy.
I wish to make this point clear. In my opinion, in the modern industrial world the only .credit base strong enough to underwrite reconstruction in the world, as a whole, or in Canada, is the productive labour of all the people in all countries, under public control. The greater need in Europe has hastened this development. The same trend1 is in evidence in the United States and in Canada. Take, for instance, the wonderful success we have had with our rubber plant at Sarnia and other state-operated plants during the war. Look at the great development of the T.V.A. and the development of the Grand Coulee dam, the Boulder dam, and other great developments which so-called free enterprise could not undertake but which were undertaken by the state in the United States and by the state in this country, and successfully prosecuted.
The world-wide extension of industry and agriculture outlined in our international declarations and obligations is rapidly making obsolete the method of private investment financing for large-scale undertakings. In addition to the compulsion of immediate needs in Europe, there is the increasing pressure of ideas expressed by socialists and democrats everywhere. There is the insistent demand for democratic processes to be expressed in economic as well as in political control.
These are inevitable measures, because anyone who studies the situation closely can see them developing and continuing to develop. These inevitable measures and developments do not inaugurate a socialist economy, despite those who shout about not lending their money to establish socialism. What is being rapidly experienced in the western section of Europe, and will inevitably develop 'here, is a form of state capitalism, gradually passing from state aid and regulations to state ownership and management of banks, key industries, transportation and public utilities.
This development will modify some features of our economy. It will be, a modified form of capitalism. It will substitute state controls over competition and invsstment for our

present largely private and monopolistic controls, but capitalist income will foe retained. Former owners of nationalized undertakings will be guaranteed fixed returns by the state.
This general development presents great opportunities. Historically, the final form of capitalist enterprise means that we have an opportunity of achieving a change from a capitalist to a socialist society in a peaceful and evolutionary way.
