The third essential is a strong cooperative movement. Social changes are not brought about merely by written programmes, speeches and national advertising. Social changes are brought about largely on a sound and solid basis, the result of the hard work of all the people who join trade unions, cooperatives and community organizations, devoting their time and energy to the building up of democracy in the smaller spheres. These are the people who really build the fabric of democracy.
The fourth essential must be a strong farmers' movement, a strong agricultural movement. I believe it is absolutely necessary, if we are to survive this dangerous stage 63260-19
in our history and in the world's history, to work as far as possible for the decentralization of administration through provincial and municipal governments. I believe it is necessary for the federal administration to lay down the general policy to balance the national interests, particularly with regard to exports in the larger sphere of planning. If we are to maintain the democratic structure we must have decentralization. We have to get the administration in the hands of the people through provincial and municipal governments, credit unions, cooperatives and all such organs of the people themselves.
Finally, I think it is necessary to have a programme to provide the opportunity for this peaceful development, and in conclusion I should like to say this. Of all the parties in this house, this is the only one that has a programme which has been considered in logical relation to the development of society at home and abroad. A study of the Regina manifesto and national programme of the C.C.F. in relation to present economic developments at home and abroad will indicate that these programmes are designed to meet the needs of the Canadian people at this time. Any person who gives intelligent study to the history of the development of economies abroad and of our own economy at home under present conditions, and who reads the Regina manifesto and the national programme of the C.C.F. party, will realize that the people who drafted that manifesto and that programme did so with an understanding and appreciation of Canadian conditions, Canadian historical background and Canadian psychology, and with a full understanding of a programme that would meet the needs of our people.

Mr. Speaker, you will allow me first, in my maiden speech in this house, to congratulate you on the consistent efficiency with which you have been discharging the duties of your high office.
I also join my distinguished colleagues in congratulating the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Viau), the mover of the Address in reply to the speech from the throne, and the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters), the seconder, for the eloquent and detailed manner in which they told us what the government intend to do during the present session.
Certain important and difficult problems will be submitted to us, especially as regards the new loan which appears to embody very favourable arrangements and generous conditions for the United Kingdom. While keeping an eye on our tremendous national debt,
1EYIBED EDITION
The Address-Mr. Gourd

we still realize the advantage of a further extraordinary effort on the part of Canada to control its foreign markets, for we must not forget that our country must export at least 40 per cent of its total production. We must have buyers and Great Britain is still our best customer. It is with this in mind that we must make it possible for her to buy our goods and, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the reorganization of our trade with England might result in keeping all classes of our people gainfully employed. I realize that this is the only means of preventing the disastrous unemployment situation that prevailed after the war of 1914-18.
Before speaking of the beautiful and immense northern part of the province of Quebec, I may be allowed to commend two others of my colleagues, the hon. members for Wright (Mr. Raymond) and Prescott (Mr. Bertrand), for having suggested that Canada should send a diplomatic representative to the Vatican, acknowledged as the greatest centre of Christianity in the world. The cooperation of a Canadian representative would help the few other ambassadors to contribute to the realization of enduring peace under the enlightened guidance of the holy father.
I wish also to congratulate the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) for his clear, accurate, and sincere statement on the Canadian flag, which should be distinctive and acceptable to all Canadians.
Now, I come to the 'constituency of Chap-leau, which I have the honour of representing and which is included in the Abitibi district, this large expanse of fertile land, well adapted to farming and stretching from Senneterre, in the east, to La Reine, in the west, on the Ontario boundary. In this region onljr a strip of land has been opened so far and settled by farmers, but it could extend to the north as far as lake Matagami, on the fiftieth and a half degree of latitude, about a hundred miles north of Amos, the county seat. In this large territory could be established a hundred farming parishes on fertile land which could supply the lumber and pulpwood so much in demand in this country. It would also contribute to the opening of mines, for mineral ores are to be found throughout the district.
The development of the north country would bring there a considerable number of people, which would relieve congestion in cities and help prevent unemployment, because the population cannot possibly be concentrated in large centres. In order to carry out the development of northern Quebec, it would also be necessary that the dominion govern-

ment should come to an agreement with the provincial authorities with a view to drawing up a comprehensive plan. There should be built a railway line, starting from the Canadian National line, either from Senneterre Junction or elsewhere, and leading northwesterly to lake Matagami and northeasterly to Chibougamou, which would help the development of water powers and facilitate the erection of a paper mill at lake Matagami. I should like to emphasize the fact that much gold, copper and other ores are to be found in the Chibougamou area. To facilitate the transportation of engineers and of the numerous mining prospectors, there should be established an air line from Montreal, with airports at Val d'Or, Amos and Noranda, from which district that line would continue on to Toronto, which now has air communications with North Bay and Ottawa. The route I suggest is several hundred miles shorter.
The governments concerned should also extend a dirt road as far as James bay covering a distance of 150 to 175 miles; this would help to bring about the above mentioned developments.
I might add that the federal government should also assist the provincial government in building highways and dredging certain rivers both of which are essential factors in the development of mines bringing in revenue which contributes to the prosperity of the country. All these projects should be included in past-war planning.
I will not conclude without outlining the income that might be derived from the implementation of these projects. Here are authentic figures relating to the tiny section already developed. In 1944, we harvested in the Abitibi district $25,150 worth of wheat, $472,540 worth of oats, $31,680 worth of barley, $2,261,500 worth ,of hay, not to mention thousands of dollars worth of buckwheat, rye, peas, beans and mixed grain. Moreover, our crop of potatoes amounted to $587,820, which does not include the income brought in by alfalfa, turnips and corn. We have also produced 1,334,209 pounds of butter, 97,747 pounds of cheese, not to mention the thousands of dollars derived from our crop of blueberries. Moreover, we sold and shipped one hundred million feet of saw lumber as well as millions of cords of pulpwood.
Neither must I forget to mention the mining of metals such as gold, copper, etc.; gold yielded a value of $42,000,000 and copper, a value of $22,000,000, these amounts being exclusive of all other minerals.
In passing, I take the occasion of suggesting to the directors of the Canadian National Railways that it is high time to improve the

The Address-Mr. Bentley
railway lines which run through our district if they want to furnish travellers with suitable means of transportation as well as take care of the shipping demand arising from the various products I have just listed.
In conclusion, I beg the Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to appoint a bilingual controller of the experimental farm located at Kapuskasing, because the majority of those whom it serves are French-Canadians.
(Text:) Mr. T. J. BENTLEY (Swift Current) : As a rule I do not take up a great deal of the time of the house, I had not expected to speak in this debate at all. As mentioned by some other members this afternoon it was felt that we might finish the debate fairly soon, but apparently that idea became sidetracked somewhere, and I felt that I should like to offer some of my opinions while the opportunity presented itself.
I was pleased this evening to hear the little battle going on between the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Grant) and the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure). It reminded me that the island was down there. I was a little surprised when the hon. member for Kings said that a map of Canada had been published that did not have Prince Edward Island on it. It is more years than I like to think of since I lived in Nova Scotia, but even back over all those years I can remember that there was a place called Prince Edward Island, so that I do not know how anyone could have forgotten it. The hon. member also said-and I hope the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) will take this seriously-that his constituency, which must be fairly small, actually had six fish docks built there, and that he expected to get two more. That is fine. We do not envy them their fish docks. No doubt they need them, or they would not get them. But I should like the minister to consider giving us one little bridge over the South Saskatchewan river at Saskatchewan Landing, at the same time he is building fish docks in Kings.
Before I say some things that may not be so pleasant, I should like to address one or two rather nice remarks to the house. At the outset I wish to join with those who have so eloquently said farewell to the Earl of Athlone and the Princess Alice, and to extend my best regards and those of my ^constituents. Our people out in Swift Current are just ordinary people, but they are warm hearted and hospitable, and on their behalf they would like me to say, in our plain way, "good-bye and good luck." While the group

I am with over here looks forward to the time when we shall form a government here, which will not be long, when the British North America Act and other necessary acts will be amended so that we shall have a Canadian citizen as governor general, until that time comes, with our usual Canadian hospitality we welcome to Canada the new governor general and his gracious consort.
While I am in a welcoming mood I should like to take this opportunity of inviting all those within sound of my voice, or who may take the trouble to read my remarks, to come to Swift Current this summer on the 1st and 2nd of July. We put on a good stampede there. They will find all the men wearing whiskers, and the ladies-^oh, we have lovely ladies out there-
Address yourself to the Prime Minister on that.

Well, yes; perhaps
particularly to the Prime Minister. The ladies will be dressed as in the days of old. I know the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) will tell the house they have a better show in his city, because it lasts for a week. Our stampede lasts for only two days, but I am sure it would be equal to a week at Calgary, so that we should like to have hon. members come there if they care to do so. The new synthetic rubber from the Sarnia plant will no doubt provide the necessary tires, and gasoline, while not free, is now plentiful. So that on behalf of Swift Current I extend this invitation to all hon. members here.
I should like also to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Viau) and the seconder (Mr. Winters) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As others have said, it always pleases those of us who are veterans of either war when a veteran is singled out for some particular honour of this kind, and these veterans really did an excellent job. I think they could be called creators. It is a long time since I took a Latin lesson, but if I remember aright the word "create" is derived from the Latin word creo, which I believe means to make out of nothing, and they did an excellent job of making a speech out of nothing, which is practically what the speech from the throne is. The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, who seconded the address, is a native of my own province, and I cannot but feel that his intelligence will so guide him that when we do form the government over there, he will still be on that side of the house. I think that would be a natural evolutionary process for such a brilliant young man.
The Address-Mr. Bentley

I wish also to express complete disapproval of the methods employed by the government in dealing with the investigation of Canadian men and women suspected of betraying secrets. Investigation was necessary. It would have been highly improper for a government not to have made an investigation; and if these people should be found guilty of giving away secrets or breaking their sacred word, they will have to be punished. But the practice of taking into custody men and women who have had no charges laid against them is, I believe, entirely wrong. I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well), the leader of our'party, and with speakers from other sides of the house who have said this was a wrong thing to do. I have grown up in this country believing that, no matter what might be the imperfections in our society, at least there was one thing we could depend upon:	that (the process of
justice which we have built up through many centuries of struggle would be kept inviolate, and that neither men nor women suspected of any crime, no matter how vicious that crime,' should be held in custody unless a definite charge was brought against them. I never believed such people could be taken into custody and placed in such a position that, unless they were strong-minded persons, they might say something which would help to convict themselves. I think the ^ government has demonstrated by this action that it has neither the ability nor the courage to safeguard the state without resorting to the practices of other governments, whom we *have just spent six years of our lives defeating, because they threatened to impose that sort of thing upon us. I say that this government, when faced with the task of protecting the state under democratic rules evolved through centuries of struggle, has fallen far short of the glory.
I should like to read the first paragraph of the speech from the throne:
It is just over six months since Canada emerged from- six long yeaTs of war. The turmoil which has followed in the wake oi^ war has created new problems for governments in all [DOT] parts of the globe. The world is full of unrest. Hunger privation and suffering have become the lot of millions. Other millions are homeless, many of them in exile.
That is fine, down to that point; not very much constructive about it, but a lot of information we can get from almost any newspaper or magazine. Then the next sentence states:
The problems which face the statesmen of every nation are formidable indeed.
In regard to Canada's contribution toward a peaceful and prosperous world, there is some

truth in that statement;'but in regard to our domestic problems, there should be no difficulty at all. We were not destroyed by war. We were nearly destroyed before the war by the depression, for which this government had no solution, although it was in power for four years before war broke out. In a land of abundant food, minerals and raw materials, people were hungry, cold and homeless, and those conditions would have continued under this government but for the war which, rather than the ingenuity of the government, opened for us a market which could and did consume everything we could produce. We speak of reconstruction, when in actual fact the needs of war and our ability to fill them brought about the reconstruction of our pre-war moribund economy.
I cannot associate myself with those who voice such fulsome praise for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe). The great generosity, loyalty and sincerity of Canadian men and women, appealed to by the publicity committees of the national, provincial and unit war finance committees; the hours of unpaid or ill-paid work during victory loan campaigns by humble citizens, regardless of party political affiliations, had a decisive result in filling the purse of the Minister of Finance, who in turn made available to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply all the financial requirements necessary to inspire profit-hungry industry to uncork the bottle of production. The reconstruction of Canada from hard years of humiliating poverty to a nation with everyone able to work on a payroll, and some not so able to work, was made possible by war, not by wise statesmen. It was the work of farm men and women with barnyard mud on their feet, factory boys and girls with grease behind their ears, lumberjacks with callouses on their hands, miners with grime on their faces, transport workers who kept the wheels of worn-out machinery rolling, fishermen with chapped and bleeding hands, dock workers with muscles in their backs and no spare tires on the front sides of their belts, merchant seamen who faced the seas and fought the enemy, and many of whom died, servicemen and women who fought or serviced the fighters, and scientists who discovered new processes.
These are the people who won the war. Before the war our present government was utterly incapable of formulating a programme of reconstruction, and now that the war is over, they are still incapable of making use of that tremendous productive power we have built up during the war.

The Address-Mr. Bentley
Then we read another paragraph in the speech from the throne, number 5 in my copy, because I have numbered them for the sake of convenience:
The -maintenance of a -high level of employment and national income is a fundamental aim of government policy.
That sounds splendid-"A high national income"; but what does the government mean by a high national income? How high is up, anyway? In the early days of the war, when the government was afraid it was not going to have the support of workers who were fed up with the kind of administration we had had, everything was promised. In those days the promise was "full employment". Them, as things settled down a little bit and industry felt itself more solid in the saddle, it became "high employment". Now it is modified to suit what I suppose the government thinks will suit the people-which it does not-and it is referred to as "a high level of employment".
I wonder why these changes were made? I wonder if it could possibly be because of some of the pronouncements by business men in this country, reference to whom was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis).
I should like to read into the record two other pronouncements carried on the editorial page of the Western Producer of July 13, 1944. The first one is attributed to a prominent banker, and if hon. members wish to have his name they may communicate with the Western Producer. Perhaps that publication will tell them, but it did not tell me. This is the quotation:
Full employment would he incompatible with the free enterprise system, which carries with it the right to a normal float of unemployed.
And the other gem, attributed to a big business man, says this:
A corporation's efficiency is indicated by the number of men it can -release from a job, not by the number of men hired.
Possibly that kind of thing has some influence with this government. Even if we get a high level of employment, what does the government mean by "high"? Is seventy per cent high? Is sixty-eight per cent high? Should it be seventy-two per cent; or what, in fact, is a "high level"? Seventy per cent is usually considered a pretty fair level when one is writing an examination in school. I think schoolteachers will agree with that.
So that if we get a high level of, let us say, seventy per cent of employment, then inversely the other thirty per cent would be-well, what would we call them? Possibly we could call them the low level of unemployment. I
suppose they will sit around with patriotic fervour and sing about the glories of a country that gives seventy per cent of their brothers and sisters employment, but leaves them without it. If they sit around long enough they will get weak enough, of course, so that they will not be able to sing about it anymore. Maybe that is the way we shall get full employment-when that thirty per cent passes out from starvation.
The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton), who is my deskmate-and incidentally the terror of the Liberal electoral machine in that constituency-dealt very ably with agriculture in his address in this debate. He, like myself and others in this group, is in constant touch with the working farmers of the west. We know their problems just as well as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) or the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) knows them. We are not political agronomists. Our contact is right with the men and women on the farms, in their homes, in their fields, in their cattle sheds and other places where they actually perform the work of production,
It was a grand battle we witnessed here this afternoon, from one side. And no doubt other hon. gentlemen on the opposite side will come back in the near future with similar ammunition. They can quote figures from now till doomsday-and undoubtedly their figures will be correct. But whether they are put in the right place so as to give a wholly true picture is a different matter. Undoubtedly there would not be much question about the number of acres or the number of bushels produced, or about those other matters which were dealt with. But I would point out that the people who raised the wheat, oats, barley, rye, flaxseed, cattle, hogs, poultry products and dairy products are not concerned with the learned battle which takes place in this House of Commons. They are concerned with policy which produces things they require, and which makes it possible for them to make their contribution in a community to people who need what they produce. They are not interested in the whole academic discussion as to who did what back in 1919, or at some other time.
If it comes to a question of who did what, I can assure hon. members that the farmers of western Canada have suffered equally under the regimes of Tory as well as Liberal administrations.	_
This afternoon the leader of the opposition made a statement with which I agree wholeheartedly. He said that never has western Canada-in fact, I believe he referred to
The Address-Mr. Bentley

agriculture in all Canada-had a square deal. That is a fact. And it does not require any long list of figures to support it.
When he was discussing this matter in this debate, the Minister of Agriculture said that he believed in planning. That is quite an admission to come from a source that champions free enterprise, when we consider that the free enterprise people of this country carried on such a round programme of condemnation of this group which had recommended that there be some kind of planning for national life.
I have never heard the Minister of Agriculture in this government, or the leader of the opposition or any of his followers deny that Mr. Trestrail and his group were friendly to them, nor have they denied that group in any way. I do not know whether they have given their actual blessing, but certainly their silence indicates that at least they have offered a covert blessing. So that when the minister said he believed in planning I felt most pleased, until he told us how his plans are to work out. He planned so well that even the most expert weather forecaster would not presume to compete with him.
Here is an example of the minister's planning. In the early thirties when the Tories were sitting on the government benches and the Liberals were on this side as the official opposition, he and his group proclaimed that there was nothing wrong with speculative marketing. There was no difference between the government and the official opposition, and there is no difference between them today, except that the government, having the load of responsibility, has had to accept the impact of logic and do a little planning. Otherwise there was no difference. They both agreed on speculative marketing. But at that time the Tory government had the load of responsibility, and they had to do something. We went through the world crash of 1929. When all the men and women and boys and girls who had a little extra money in 1929 and could speculate in wheat and options went broke and had no more wages or salaries or no more profits from their little businesses they disappeared as speculative buyers, and the result was that there was no longer any speculative market to make our open market system buoyant, as the phrase is. The government, charged with responsibility, were then forced by the impact of logic to introduce what they called their stabilization operations, and every taxpayer of this dominion, through the treasury, was put behind this plan of hypothecation for the sake of saving the speculative market through
rMr. Bentley.]
stabilization operations. I am not going to be too critical of that because at least the government did something to try to relieve the situation. But they got no credit for that from the present Minister of Agriculture or from his friends.
When the present minister became Minister of Agriculture at Ottawa in 1935 he proceeded to plan to do the things that he had said were necessary before he got that job. "Get rid of surpluses" was the cry, "and then we will get dollar wheat, and dollar wheat will pay your taxes." That was the great cry at that time-get rid of surpluses. How we would like to have ten times those surpluses in our bins at the present time, Mr. Speaker, so that we would be able to say to people in other parts of the world: Here is lots of wheat and lots of oats and lots of barley; and they would have been ready to pay more for it than some of the speculative markets did. I have bought barley at country elevators in western Canada for one and a half cents a bushel because the man who had it could not bother taking it back home with him and he said, "I might as well sell it for one and a half cents." Some barley had no quotations on it at all. You could buy good feed oats for eight cents a bushel, and the -most you could get in some years for the best oats was from thirteen to seventeen cents a bushel.
So what?

So what? We felt just as the hon. member for Fraser Valley would feel if his orchards were full of fruit and there was no market for it, and he was forced to sell at ten cents a box. We do not like to be in that position. We did not like it then. At no time have the western farmers liked to be in that position, no more than anybody else wants to sc* his means of livelihood drop to such a low level. But if we had those surpluses now, should we not be glad? But when the present Minister of Agriculture came into office in this government in 1935 he proceeded to get rid of surpluses, and his planning, along with associations and possibly some occult powers, and nature, helped him to get rid of the surplus.
The year 1937 came along and no wheat was raised. His cry had always been: Get rid of surpluses and the price of wheat will go up. So 1937 came, and no crop. He and nature had worked well together. Nature did not produce any rain and the Minister of Agriculture and the other farmers did not produce any crops. The surplus disappeared, and the price of wheat did go up to SI a bushel.

The Address-Mr. Bentley
In the spring of 1938 the minister and nature did better. By that time the farmers had to buy seed grain back at $1.45 a bushel. Yes, the price of wheat had gone up, but nobody can say that that was the way to bring prosperity to the farmers, to have them pay $1.45 a bushel for seed grain and receive sometimes only eighteen cents a bushel when they sold that wheat. That is the basis of the seed grain debt in Saskatchewan to-day.
But the Minister of Agriculture, like the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe), is nothing if not an optimist. He believed that the future was going to do something better for him and the country. He said: We have got rid of the surplus; we have $1.45 wheat, and now what we need is a crop. Nature said, O.K., we shall have a crop, and so in 1938 nature and the minister produced us a crop, not a very good crop; it did not create a very big surplus, but it was more than the market was prepared to handle, and down went the price of wheat. Instead of being looked upon as a blessing it was looked upon as a curse, instead of nature's bounty. Down went the price again and remained that way until the farmers of western Canada had to take action themselves and come here to Ottawa and petition the government for some relief. That was long after the war had started. We believe in planning, but certainly we do not appreciate the particular type of planning that brought those results. Certainly planning is necessary. All through the years I have been associated with the kind of farmers I mentioned, not political agricultural experts such as we see in the house, but the men that actually operate the tractors, the combines and the seeders. That is the kind of man that I have worked alongside; I know what they want and what they need, and they know what they want and what they need. They have farm organizations and they believe in planning. I am not suggesting that I represent those farm organizations, so let no one here try to make capital out of that. These farm organizations are distinctly non-political, but from eighteen years of association with that kind of organization I know their story; I know something of their hopes and aspirations, and I know the kind of planning which they had hoped would be done and the kind of representations which they have made to this and other governments to have that kind of planning put into operation.
Here is a report from the Saskatchewan wheat pool, which every year issues a written report. After dealing with certain things which they would like to have had but which
they failed to convince the federal government to do, they go on to say in their annual report for 1941:
The government wheat policy to date has been *a policy of inflexible opposition to the recommendations of representative farm organizations.
That report was laid before the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool in November, 1941, over two years after the war had started, _ and that organization, which is completely non-political, after trying in vain to have its programme accepted by the powers that be, whether Liberal, Tory or anything else, was finally forced to report back to its members that this government's policy was a policy of inflexible opposition to the recommendations of representative farm organizations. That does not look like very smart planning, if it is planning at all, having in mind the position of the organized producer.
Then there is another plan which the minister was telling us about the other day in his speech. I do not know whether he was trying to "kid" us or himself, or whether he has a great sense of humour. He introduced his acreage reduction plan. The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton) showed here a poster which said in plain terms, "Grow less wheat and win the war", and it had on it, "By authority of the Minister of Agriculture." I cannot believe that the minister would permit those posters to be put up if he knew his name was on them and disapproved of their being shown.
I wrote it and put my name on it.

Good; we have that admission. That is a wonderful start for another plan, "Grow less wheat and win the war". I am told that during the last war- I was not here at the time-there was a great drive put on under the slogan, "Grow more wheat and win the war". In this war it is, "Grow less wheat and win the war." There is a kind of stock joke in Saskatchewan-I do not know about the other provinces-which runs like this: In the year 1958 a child climbs on its daddy's knee and says, "Daddy, what did you do to help win world war No. 2?" And daddy says, "My son, I raised less wheat; I summer-fallowed."

Will my hon. friend
allow me to ask him a question?
If you do not take my time, I will; otherwise I would suggest what Mr. Speaker always tells us to do, put it on the order paper.

My hon. friend spoke of a resolution passed by the Saskatchewan
The Address-Mr. Bentley

wheat pool in 1941. I wonder if he would read the one which was passed at their last board meeting.

I have that, but I have not time to read it to-night. We shall do so later on.
The minister said that he planned well. If he planned to reduce wheat production, why does he take credit for the fact that in 1942, following the wheat acreage reduction plan, we had the biggest crop of wheat the country ever had? Where did the plan go astray?
I have only a little time left, and there are some other things I should like to have dealt with.
Oh, oh.
It is all right. You will get an opportunity, and you will probably go overtime a little bit and will get the unanimous consent of the house to do so.
Go ahead.

No, I will not if I can avoid doing so. I wish to mention one or two matters in connection with labour. We have, of course, in our group men who are thoroughly conversant with all labour problems, and I am not going to try to deal with those matters. But I wish to make known to the house the plight of a certain group of labour people in the west; I do not believe the same condition affects employees in the east. They are workers of the Canadian Pacific railway, and either because they wanted to strike or were inadvertently drawn into a strike away back in 1918 and 1919, they are now being laid off and retired at the age of sixty-five without the benefit of any retirement fund. I do not suppose that this government has any authority to order the CR.R. to do anything to correct the evil. The strike happened at a time when we had a labour-hating government-which I believe was not a Liberal government-and of course a labour-hating management, or they would not have done what they did. In any event these men are in that position; and I believe that this house could, if it so desired, persuade, or instruct, or whatever this house does to the government when the house really wants something done by it, that it set up some kind of fund which would give these men the same superannuation allowances to which they would have been entitled had this condition not been applied. I suggest that this is an excellent opportunity for the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. 
Usley) to get together. The Minister of Labour could labour and produce a plan, and the Minister of Finance could exercise those marvellous qualities we are always hearing about, and finance it. Then everybody would be happy, and I believe the Canadian people generally would be glad to see these men properly taken care of. I hope the Minister of Labour will give, not only serious consideration and an investigation by some departmental employee, but actual serious departmental consideration and government official consideration in correcting the situation.
I have about exhausted my time. I am sorry I cannot see in the speech from the throne the many bright hues which have been mentioned by others. If we were a bunch of Hollywood people discussing a script that had come out, probably I would make the remark that the government had "laid an egg"; but I do not know that that would be appropriate, .for an egg is an important item of food at the present time if it is fresh, and if it is not fresh there are other uses to which it may be put, notably at election times. This speech from the throne is something like what used to be done when I was a child back home on the farm. They used to find some kind of lime egg, and sometimes an old discarded white door-knob, and put it in the nest to lure the reluctant hen to come up on the nest. I think what the government has done in the speech from the throne in this. It has put the hen on a door-knob and now it hopes to hatch out a house and lot.

Mr. Speaker, now that the votes have been taken on two amendments, one of which was moved by the Conservative party, and the other by the C.C.F., on behalf of the "Social Credit group I wish to move another one, one that we consider to be essential to the welfare of the Canadian people.
Before doing so, however, I wish to make a few comments regarding the speech from the throne. I think hon. members of the C.C.F. party will appreciate the reason we could not support their amendment. It was for the very simple reason that we did not have a mandate from the people of Alberta to support the establishment of a socialist state.

The Address-Mr. Quelch
Whilst the Conservative party may think there was nothing in their proposals that we could object to, let me point out that their proposals were absolutely hamstrung by their declared financial policy. I should like to remind the house of what that policy is, in part, as declared in the budget debate of last year by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell). I refer hon. members to page 1296 of Hansard of 1945 where the hon. member said:
So far as expenditure is concerned we must make up our minds, based upon the best estimate we can make of the national income, how much of this income can be safely taken by the state; having made up our minds on this, we must then make a heroic effort to keep our expenditure within that amount.
That declaration, Mr. Speaker, in the opinion of this group is a policy of reaction. It recalls to mind the policies of the former minister of finance, the Hon. Charles Dunning, under whose policies from 1935 to 1939 the resources of this country were systematically sabotaged as a result of curtailing expenditures in an attempt to balance the budget. It will be recalled that during those years the minister always insisted that the only money which was available to the government was the money that they could obtain from the people's pockets, and as a consequence we allowed over half a million people to remain unemployed and a million people to be on relief. So much for the Conservative policy.
What of the government's policy in this regard? I have already referred to their pre-war deflationary policy. But the house will recall the very sudden change that took place in government policy immediately after the declaration of war. It will be recalled that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated soon after the declaration of the war that no financial restrictions would be allowed to impede the government's war effort, that the only limit to our war effort would be a physical one, that of the number of men and materials that were available to execute it. That declaration received the whole-hearted endorsation of the people of Canada from one end to the other and received the whole-hearted endorsation of the members of this house. .
I would also remind hon. members that when we in this group from 1935 to 1939 had also made a similar declaration, a declaration of a realistic policy, namely, that whatever was physically possible and desirable should also be made financially possible, that declaration was ridiculed not only by members on the other side but by members in 63260-20J
other parts of the house. It was not until the fear of war struck the government that they were willing to adopt what might be called a realistic policy. Well, to-day the war is over, but once again we are reverting to pre-war policies. Surely it must be quite plain that if a realistic policy is necessary and justified in order to win the war, a realistic policy should be justified in order to win the peace. I say that for this reason. Winning the war is not the ultimate objective. Winning the war is merely the first major objective that must be captured in order that we may go on to the ultimate objective, that of winning a permanent peace, a peace that will have some permanency attached to it, and the only kind of peace that can have any permanency attached to it is one that will make it possible for peoples in all countries in the world to live in the greatest degree of freedom, free from the fear of want and aggression, free to live their lives as they choose; that freedom itself covers all other freedoms. Certainly, if that is to be the objective of the world, then Canada is in an admirable position to give leadership along these lines. But I would ask, do we find that type of leadership in the speech from the throne? I think it can very well be shown that we find therein to a very large extent a repetition of those policies that were put into force not only in this country but in all the highly industrialized nations throughout the world between the two great wars and even prior to 1914.
The speech from the throne makes it quite clear that in order to maintain full employment and a high standard of living the government depends very largely upon exports, depends very largely upon a programme of foreign investment. While it must be quite clear that exporting wealth without bringing back the equivalent in the form of imports may help to maintain a programme of full employment, it must be equally clear, on the other hand, that it will not maintain the standard of living of the people at the highest level possible because, when you ship wealth out of a country without bringing back imports to a similar amount, you are bound to reduce the standard of living to the extent that you have that unbalance.
We in this group quite agree that we have a moral obligation to make available to the areas that have been made destitute by war all the goods that we can spare. We are, for example, thoroughly behind the government's proposal for a loan to Britain. But I wish to point out that this is entirely different from a programme of foreign investment as
